newsitem.title: FRANCE: Daewoo not ruled out as Thomson suitor.
newsitem.headline: Daewoo not ruled out as Thomson suitor.

text.p: French finance minister Jean Arthuis said on Thursday that Daewoo Electronics could still be a candidate to buy Thomson Multimedia but it would depend on the way the consumer electronics group was privatised.
He told reporters there was "no reason why Daewoo should be excluded" from the list of suitors but that it "would depend on the formula" used for the privatisation.

Relaunching the privatisation of defence and consumer electronics group Thomson SA suspended last week, the government announced late Wednesday it would sell it in two parts after originally planning to dispose of it in one go.

It will sell defence subsidiary Thomson CSF "in the early months of 1997". Money-losing Thomson Multimedia would be sold off later after implementation of a recovery plan and an 10 billion franc recapitalisation. It gave no exact timetable.

The government's announcement followed a U-turn last week in which it scrapped Thomson SA's sale to Lagardere after the privatisation commission opposed the terms of Lagardere's plan to spin off Thomson Multimedia to Daewoo.
Arthuis said the government had not decided whether the privatisations would be through a company-to-company sale as previously planned or a public share offering.

Daewoo has been quoted as saying it still is interested in buying Thomson Multimedia but most likely at a lower price than the 7.1 billion francs it was reported to have originally offered given the delays and the company's troubles.
Engineering and telecommunications group Alcatel Alsthom is interested in the privatisation of Thomson-CSF but is waiting to see the terms, an Alcatel spokesman said on Thursday.

Arthuis, meanwhile, sought to appease outraged South Korean feelings over the cancelled sale, saying "the quality of the candidates was never in doubt". Korean industry has slammed the decision as unfair and discriminatory.

Arthuis added he hoped the move would not send out the wrong message. "France cannot develop without being open to the rest of the world," he said, adding that he was aware of the damage to France's image. "It cannot retreat into itself," he said.
